content: Chain Volume Measure (CVM) is an index number used in statistical publications, such as those reporting Gross Domestic Product (GDP), to facilitate comparisons of data across different time periods. The selection of a base year for these comparisons is critical. Fixed-base aggregations compare data from one period to another, such as GDP growth in 2006 compared to a base year of 2001. However, this method has limitations because the relevance of the base year diminishes over time as the composition of goods and services changes. For instance, video cassette recorders might have been significant in 2000 but irrelevant by 2006, making fixed-base comparisons less accurate. To address this issue, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the United Kingdom introduced chained volume measures (CVM). This approach allows for more frequent updates to the base year, improving the accuracy of statistical comparisons. Instead of revising the base year every five years, as was previously the case, CVM updates the base year annually. Calculations are performed using prices from the previous year, and these are aggregated to produce the chain volume measures. The ONS has replaced the term constant prices with CVM in its terminology to describe GDP components. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) implemented changes in the September quarter of 1998 to align with new international standards outlined in the System of National Accounts 1993 (SNA93). One significant change was the adoption of a single measure of GDP growth in real terms. This involved replacing constant price estimates, which remove the effects of price changes, with chain volume measures. Previously, constant price estimates were based on a fixed base year, such as the financial year 1989-90. While expressed in dollar terms, these estimates only reflected changes in underlying quantities, as prices were held constant. A major criticism of constant price estimates is their declining accuracy as the current period moves further from the base year. This is due to substantial changes in the relative prices of goods and services over time. Different methods for deriving constant price estimates yield varying results depending on the extent of relative price changes. If all prices increase at the same rate, the methods produce consistent results. However, in reality, some prices rise faster than others, and some fall while others increase. Greater variation in relative price changes leads to larger discrepancies in constant price estimates, moving them further from the true real value. This phenomenon is known as the substitution effect, where items with rapidly increasing prices are replaced by relatively cheaper alternatives. For example, computing equipment has experienced significant price declines and increased quantities in recent years, leading to an overstatement of growth in constant price estimates. The key question is how frequently constant price series should be rebased to minimize the substitution effect. Historically, constant price estimates were rebased approximately every five years. However, SNA93 recommends annual rebasing, a practice now adopted by the ABS in line with leading statistical agencies worldwide. Chain volume measures, like constant price estimates, are expressed in dollar terms. By rebasing annually, CVM ensures that price relativities reflect the current situation, providing more accurate real estimates, particularly during periods of rapidly changing relative prices. With annual rebasing, the base year for chain volume measures changes each year. For example, with the release of September quarter 1998 data, the base year was 1996-97. The release of June quarter 1999 figures used a base year of 1997-98, and the base year will continue to change annually with the release of June quarter data. When a new base year is introduced, the level of the chain volume measures series will change, but growth rates will remain consistent unless influenced by other factors. In cases where constant price series were previously used, the corresponding chain volume measure series should now be adopted.
